title: The short books, closed
hook: the Sutta Nipata, the Udana, the Itivuttaka

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Itivuttaka's last discourse, and your line, as he speaks, so he does. Did a word and a deed line up? Today we close the short books and look back. Day six hundred thirty-five.

Some of the best things people say are short. A grandparent's one line at a wedding. A note left on the fridge. A verse someone copied onto a card and kept in a wallet for years. These last weeks lived in books like that. Not the long discourses, with their journeys and debates, but three small collections of verses and sayings, some of them only a few lines long. They're shelved together in the Pali canon's Khuddaka Nikaya, the collection of short texts. Today we close them. Today: the short books.
screen: `A NOTE ON THE FRIDGE.` → `A VERSE KEPT IN A WALLET.` → `WEEKS OF SHORT BOOKS.`

segments.voice: First, the Sutta Nipata, which some scholars count among the earliest Buddhist poetry. It opened with a monk shedding the world like a snake sheds its skin. We walked alone like the rhinoceros horn, or with a good friend. We read the discourse on kindness again, the jewel discourse, and the highest blessings, from caring for parents to a mind unshaken. A boat, the dart of grief, the chapter of eights, and the long road to the far shore. Second, the Udana, inspired sayings, words the Buddha spoke when something moved him. In the seen, only the seen. Boys tormenting fish. The blind men each holding a part of the elephant. And the rare, quiet line, because there is, an escape is known. Third, the Itivuttaka, thus it was said: sayings remembered, the tradition says, by a woman who heard them and repeated them for others. Share even the last bite. Two bright guardians, conscience and concern. The whirlpool ahead. Parents as first teachers. Effort is alive. And word and deed made one. What do the three books share? They're compact. A whole teaching fits in a breath or two. They're made to be memorized and chanted, and some still are. And they're not shallow for being short. Short sayings ask more of the listener. A long discourse explains itself. A short verse leaves room, and you have to step into it. Tomorrow a very different kind of book begins, thousands of discourses sorted by subject. The short books stay on the shelf, ready.
screen: `THE SUTTA NIPATA: OLD POEMS` · `THE UDANA: INSPIRED SAYINGS` · `THE ITIVUTTAKA: THUS IT WAS SAID` · `SHORT SAYINGS ASK MORE OF YOU` · then, large: `SHORT AND DEEP.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let these last weeks drift past: the snake's skin, the rhinoceros, the jewel, the boat, the elephant, the whirlpool, the first teachers. Don't try to remember them all. Wait for one to stay. Whichever comes back on its own, that's your favorite, at least today. Let it sit in the mind, and say its line quietly to yourself, as short as you can make it. Breathe with it. After the bell, if you like, go back and reread it. The bell holds the time.
Khuddaka, small or short. The Sutta Nipata, the Udana and the Itivuttaka, three small collections of verse and saying from the Khuddaka Nikaya: short, and deep. Today's word.
Your line: short and deep. Carry one short line from these weeks with you today, and say it once when you need it. Day six hundred thirty-five.

howItsDone: Verses from the Sutta Nipata, such as the discourse on kindness, the jewel discourse and the highest blessings, are among the texts Theravada communities chant regularly, and some Buddhists learn short sayings from these books by heart.

original.note: Pali khuddaka: small, short. the Khuddaka Nikaya is the collection of short texts.

trapdoor: what you thought: the short books are a summary of the long ones.
what it means: three small collections, the Sutta Nipata, the Udana and the Itivuttaka, of verses and sayings that stand on their own.

what a scholar hears: parts of the Sutta Nipata, especially the chapter of eights and the way to the far shore, are counted by some scholars among the oldest strata of the canon; the Itivuttaka's frame story credits the laywoman Khujjuttara.

notes: Block close: the look-back names days 576–634 by their outline titles; please check the summaries match what those scripts taught (e.g. 'two bright guardians' as conscience and concern, hiri and ottappa; 'the pull home'; 'each held a part' as the blind men and the elephant).
The attribution of the Itivuttaka to the laywoman Khujjuttara is from the commentary; flagged as 'the tradition says'.
'Many scholars count among the oldest Buddhist poetry' is a softened scholarly claim; confirm.
howItsDone: confirm that the Karaniya Metta, Ratana and Mangala suttas (all in the Sutta Nipata) are commonly chanted, e.g. as paritta.
